triage.name: Diarrhea
triage.reason: Extremely common symptom with a structured history, hydration assessment and a wide infectious and non-infectious differential.

age.peak: bimodal: young children and adults of any age

demographics: Adults in the US average about one episode of acute diarrhea per year; young children average about two
More severe and more often dehydrating at the extremes of age

risk_factors.text: Contact with a household member or childcare contact who has diarrhea
Recent travel to an area with unsafe drinking water
Eating food that may have been improperly stored or handled
Lactose intolerance or another food intolerance
Known inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome
Gastric or intestinal surgery in the past

family_history: Inflammatory bowel disease in a first-degree relative
social_history: Travel outside the US in the past few weeks
Work or attendance in childcare, school, or a group living setting
Swimming in lakes, rivers, or untreated pools
exposures: Household pets or farm animals with diarrhea
Raw or undercooked meat, eggs, or unpasteurized dairy

chief_complaints.text: I keep having to run to the bathroom

hpi.onset: Sudden or gradual over hours to a day; often the patient can point to when it started
hpi.duration: Acute episodes usually last 1–3 days; chronic diarrhea is defined as lasting 4 weeks or more
hpi.progression: Loose stools increase in frequency over the first day or two, then gradually firm up and space out as the episode resolves
hpi.location: Cramping is felt in the mid-abdomen or lower abdomen, often relieved by a bowel movement
hpi.quality: Watery or mushy stools; abdominal discomfort is crampy and comes in waves
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; patients describe urgency and frequency more than pain
hpi.timing: Day and night; may wake the patient from sleep during an acute infectious episode
aggravating: Eating, especially dairy or fatty foods

associated_symptoms.text: Urgency to get to the bathroom
Blood or mucus in the stool

pertinent_negatives: Blood or pus in the stool
No urine output for many hours
Symptoms that only occur at night and wake the patient from sleep (in chronic cases)

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot describe symptoms; parents report increased stool frequency, irritability, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, and lethargy. Dehydration develops faster than in older children.
Children often have vomiting and fever along with diarrhea and can become dehydrated quickly; they may refuse to drink and have fewer wet diapers.
May have less abdominal pain and fever but more risk of dehydration, electrolyte problems, and confusion; symptoms can be blunted even with serious infection.
Diarrhea can be more severe, prolonged, and caused by unusual organisms; fever may be absent or blunted.
Dehydration and electrolyte loss can affect the pregnancy; listeriosis should be considered with fever and flu-like symptoms.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, well hydrated; able to converse and drink normally
general.moderate: Mildly tired and thirsty, slightly restless, dry mouth but interactive
general.severe: Lethargic or irritable, sunken eyes, markedly thirsty or refusing fluids, cool extremities
general.critical: Obunded or unresponsive, limp, mottled and cold, barely responsive to stimulation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa
Inspect the eyes for sunkenness and tear production
findings.finding: Sunken eyes with absent or reduced tears

findings.maneuver: Press the fingertip or nail bed for 5 seconds and release
Pinch the skin over the abdomen or forearm and release
findings.finding: Skin stays tented and returns slowly

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants lightly and deeply
findings.finding: Mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness without localization

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the abdomen in all four quadrants
Palpate the abdomen and assess for involuntary guarding or rigidity
findings.finding: No guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness
No liver or spleen enlargement, no abdominal mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam when bleeding, tenesmus, or chronic symptoms are present
findings.finding: No mass, no gross blood, normal sphincter tone

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for rash, flushing, or urticaria
Assess orientation and level of alertness

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Most common cause of acute watery diarrhea; often with vomiting, low-grade fever, and sick contacts

labs: Stool studies not needed if mild and non-bloody

differential.name: Bacterial colitis
differential.why_considered: Invasive bacteria such as Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or E. coli O157:H7 cause bloody diarrhea with fever and severe cramps
differential.trigger: Blood or pus in the stool, high fever, or severe abdominal pain

labs: Stool leukocytes or positive stool culture/PCR
Hemolytic uremic syndrome labs if E. coli O157:H7 suspected
imaging: Abdominal CT may show colonic wall thickening if severe

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
differential.why_considered: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, often watery with cramps and fever; can progress to pseudomembranous colitis
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic use or hospitalization with watery diarrhea

labs: Positive stool C. difficile toxin or PCR
imaging: CT showing colonic wall thickening and pericolonic stranding

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease flare
differential.why_considered: Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis can present with chronic or recurrent diarrhea, cramps, and bloody stools

history: Chronic diarrhea lasting weeks to months
imaging: CT or MRI enterography showing bowel wall thickening

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic or recurrent diarrhea with abdominal pain, often alternating with constipation, without alarm features

history: Symptoms for months, often alternating diarrhea and constipation
No weight loss, no blood, no nocturnal symptoms
imaging: Not routinely indicated; colonoscopy if alarm features

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss triggered by gluten; can present at any age

history: Chronic diarrhea with bloating and gas
Weight loss or failure to thrive
labs: Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy

differential.name: Lactose intolerance
differential.why_considered: Osmotic diarrhea, bloating, and gas after dairy intake; common in adults

history: Symptoms after milk or dairy products

differential.name: Medication-induced diarrhea
differential.why_considered: Antibiotics, magnesium-containing antacids, metformin, colchicine, and chemotherapy can cause diarrhea

differential.name: Giardiasis
differential.why_considered: Parasitic infection causing prolonged watery diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption; often from contaminated water

history: Travel to endemic areas or hiking/camping with untreated water
Prolonged watery diarrhea with bloating and foul-smelling stools
labs: Stool microscopy or antigen test positive for Giardia

differential.name: Ischemic colitis
differential.why_considered: Older adults with sudden abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea, often after hypotension or vascular disease
differential.trigger: Older adult with acute severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea

history: Sudden onset of crampy abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea
History of vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, or hypotension
Pain often out of proportion to exam initially
imaging: CT showing colonic wall thickening, thumbprinting, or pneumatosis

severity.mild: Acute, self-limited: 1-3 loose stools per day, no dehydration, able to drink, no fever or low-grade fever, symptoms resolve in 1-3 days
severity.moderate: More frequent stools, mild dehydration (dry mucous membranes, thirst), low-grade fever, some abdominal cramping, able to take oral fluids
severity.severe: Frequent watery stools, signs of moderate to severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, skin tenting), fever, vomiting, unable to keep up with fluid losses
severity.critical: Profound dehydration or hypovolemic shock, altered mental status, hypotension, tachycardia, minimal urine output; may occur with severe infectious colitis, toxic megacolon, or cholera-like illness

red_flags.finding: Blood or pus in the stool
red_flags.meaning: Invasive bacterial infection, inflammatory bowel disease, or ischemic colitis; needs evaluation
Systemic infection or colitis; consider bacterial cause or C. difficile

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain or peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Surgical emergency such as perforation, toxic megacolon, or ischemia

red_flags.finding: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, skin tenting, lethargy)
red_flags.meaning: Needs immediate IV fluids and evaluation

red_flags.finding: Inability to keep down fluids or persistent vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Risk of worsening dehydration; may need IV fluids

red_flags.finding: No urine output for many hours

red_flags.meaning: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding; not typical of diarrhea but requires urgent workup

red_flags.finding: Diarrhea lasting more than 2 days in adults or more than 24 hours in children
red_flags.meaning: May indicate a more serious cause or complication

complications.name: Hemolytic uremic syndrome
clues: Bloody diarrhea followed by anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure
Most common with E. coli O157:H7 in children

special_populations.differences: Dehydration develops very rapidly; parents report fewer wet diapers, irritability, poor feeding, and lethargy. Oral rehydration solution is preferred; avoid plain water.
Often have vomiting and fever; can become dehydrated quickly. Use oral rehydration solutions; monitor for decreased urine output and lethargy.
May have blunted symptoms but higher risk of dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and confusion. Lower threshold for IV fluids and hospitalization.
Dehydration and electrolyte loss can affect the pregnancy; consider listeriosis with fever and flu-like symptoms. Avoid unnecessary medications.
Diarrhea can be more severe, prolonged, and caused by unusual organisms; fever may be absent. Lower threshold for stool studies and imaging.

key_questions.question: When did the diarrhea start, and how long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Under 4 weeks suggests an acute, usually infectious or medication-related cause; 4 weeks or more defines chronic diarrhea and shifts the differential toward malabsorption, inflammatory, or functional disease

key_questions.question: How many stools a day, and what do they look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequency and character: watery, mushy, greasy and floating, or small-volume with mucus; helps separate secretory, osmotic, inflammatory, and malabsorptive patterns

key_questions.question: Is there blood, pus, or mucus in the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Visible blood or mucus points to invasive bacterial colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, or ischemic colitis rather than a simple viral or osmotic cause

key_questions.question: How much are you drinking, and how much urine are you making?
key_questions.looking_for: Ability to keep up with losses; markedly reduced urine output or inability to drink signals dehydration that needs fluids

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics in the past two months, or been in a hospital or nursing facility?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure raises concern for Clostridioides difficile infection

key_questions.question: What other medicines are you taking, including over-the-counter ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Magnesium-containing antacids, laxatives, metformin, colchicine, chemotherapy, and proton pump inhibitors can all cause diarrhea

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, or been around anyone else with diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Travel to areas with unsafe water suggests traveler's diarrhea or a parasite; sick contacts or daycare exposure suggest a viral cause

key_questions.question: What have you eaten or drunk in the last day or two, including water sources?
key_questions.looking_for: Improperly stored food, undercooked meat or eggs, unpasteurized dairy, or untreated water points to a foodborne or waterborne cause

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Crampy pain relieved by a bowel movement fits an infectious or functional cause; severe constant pain or peritoneal features suggests a surgical problem

key_questions.question: Any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever of 102°F or higher suggests invasive infection or colitis rather than a mild viral illness

key_questions.question: Any vomiting, and can you keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent vomiting that prevents drinking raises the risk of dehydration and may require IV fluids

key_questions.question: Do you have any long-term bowel condition, or has this happened before?
key_questions.looking_for: Known inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome changes the likely cause and the workup

key_questions.question: Has your weight changed without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight loss with chronic diarrhea suggests malabsorption, celiac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease

key_questions.question: Does the diarrhea wake you from sleep at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal diarrhea suggests an organic cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome

key_questions.question: Does it happen after you eat dairy or certain foods?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms after milk or dairy suggest lactose intolerance or another food intolerance

key_questions.question: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes the risk assessment and the safety of medications; fever with flu-like symptoms raises concern for listeriosis

key_questions.question: Any rash, flushing, or hives with the diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Flushing or rash would point away from a simple infectious cause toward a systemic or hormonal cause

reasoning_points: Duration separates acute from chronic diarrhea and drives the differential
Stool character and frequency describe the pattern: watery, greasy, inflammatory, or small-volume
Presence of blood, mucus, high fever, or severe pain suggests invasive or inflammatory disease
Hydration status and urine output determine urgency of fluid replacement
Medication review, especially recent antibiotics, identifies C. difficile and drug-induced causes
Travel, food, water, and sick contacts point to an infectious source
Weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, and chronicity suggest malabsorption or inflammatory bowel disease
Red flags such as peritoneal signs, black stools, or inability to drink require urgent evaluation

easy: Healthy adult with a short, self-limited watery diarrhea after a sick contact
No blood, no high fever, mild cramping, able to drink
Mild dehydration at most on exam
medium: Recent antibiotic course with watery diarrhea and cramps suggesting C. difficile
Traveler returning from an area with unsafe water with prolonged watery stools
Older adult with several days of diarrhea and lightheadedness on standing
hard: Older adult with sudden severe pain and bloody diarrhea suggesting ischemic colitis
Chronic diarrhea with weight loss and anemia suggesting malabsorption or inflammatory bowel disease
Immunocompromised patient with prolonged diarrhea and no fever
Infant with irritability, poor feeding, and fewer wet diapers where dehydration is the main concern
